The irreversible anthropogenic perturbation of the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024), manifest in geomorphological transformations (Nixon, 2011), has garnered terminological acknowledgment through the neologism 'Anthropocene' (Moore, 2016), initially proposed by Stoermer and Crutzen in 2000 (Nixon, 2011). Their revision of geological nomenclature (Smith & Zeder, 2013) entails the introduction of the 'Anthropocene epoch', intended to supplant the Holocene epoch (Haraway, 2016), thereby emphasizing the unprecedented biophysical dominance exerted by the Anthropos from the onset of the industrial era (Nixon, 2011). This paradigmatic shift in geological thought (Barnosky et al., 2011) seeks to underscore the profound impact of human activities on the Earth's systems, precipitating a new era of anthropogenic influence (Witze, 2024).

The Anthropocene epoch is characterized by a distinct set of geological features, including the widespread presence of anthropogenic sedimentation (Kemp, 2011), the alteration of natural habitats (Lamb, 2013), and the modification of global climate patterns (IPCC, 2013). This epochal transition is marked by a profound reorganization of the Earth's biophysical systems, resulting in a novel configuration of human-environmental interactions (Haraway, 2016). The Anthropocene epoch represents a critical juncture in the Earth's history, underscoring the need for a revised understanding of human relationships with the natural world (Barnosky et al., 2011).

Furthermore, the Anthropocene epoch has significant implications for our understanding of the Earth's systems and the role of human activities within them. The introduction of the Anthropocene epoch highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex interactions between human societies and the natural environment (Witze, 2024). This new paradigmatic framework seeks to integrate insights from various disciplines, including geology, ecology, and sociology, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the Earth's biophysical systems (Smith & Zeder, 2013).

In conclusion, the Anthropocene epoch represents a significant shift in our understanding of the Earth's biophysical systems and the role of human activities within them. The introduction of this new epochal framework underscores the need for a revised understanding of human relationships with the natural world and highlights the importance of integrating insights from various disciplines to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the Earth's systems.
